cards.q: Which CPU register holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched?
cards.why: The PC keeps the CPU's place in the program: it holds the address of the next instruction. The CIR holds the instruction itself once it has been fetched.
cards.hook: PC: it points to where the next instruction is, not the instruction.
keys: the address of the next instruction

cards.q: Which register holds the address of the memory location the CPU is about to read from or write to?
cards.why: The MAR holds the address: where in memory. The MDR holds the data or instruction travelling to or from that address.
cards.hook: The letter tells you: MAR = Address, MDR = Data.

cards.q: During a fetch, the instruction arrives from RAM. Which register does it go into first?
cards.why: Everything read from memory lands in the MDR first. It is then copied to the CIR to be decoded. The MAR only held the address it came from.
cards.hook: All data in or out of memory passes through the MDR.

cards.q: Which part of the CPU does the arithmetic and logic, such as adding 5 + 3 or checking whether A > B?
cards.why: The ALU is the calculator: it adds, subtracts and compares. The control unit decodes instructions and directs the rest; the accumulator only stores the result.
cards.hook: ALU does the maths; the CU is the manager telling it what to do.

cards.q: The instruction ADD 5 has just been copied into the CIR. Which part works out what it means, and which part does the adding?
wrong: CU decodes it and adds it
cards.why: The control unit decodes the instruction and sends signals to carry it out; the ALU does the arithmetic. The CIR and ACC are registers: they only hold values.
cards.hook: CU = the manager (decode, give orders); ALU = the calculator.
keys: The control unit decodes the instruction

cards.q: What are the three stages the CPU repeats for every instruction, in order?
cards.why: The CPU fetches the next instruction from memory, decodes it to work out what it means, then executes it, billions of times a second.
cards.hook: You can't carry it out (execute) before you know what it says (decode).
keys: decodes it to work out what it means

cards.q: Put the fetch stage in order: (1) the MDR is copied to the CIR, (2) the PC is copied to the MAR, (3) the instruction comes from memory into the MDR.
cards.why: First the PC's address goes to the MAR (2), then the instruction at that address comes into the MDR (3), then it is copied to the CIR to be decoded (1).
cards.hook: Address out, data in, then into the CIR.
keys: the PC's address goes to the MAR (2)

cards.q: The PC holds 25 when a fetch begins. When the fetch has finished, what do the PC and the MAR hold?
cards.why: The PC's 25 is copied to the MAR, the instruction at 25 is fetched, then the PC goes up by 1 to 26, ready for the next instruction.
cards.hook: Copy the PC first, then add 1 to it.
keys: then the PC goes up by 1 to 26

cards.q: The CPU writes the value 42 into memory address 100. What travels along the address bus and the data bus?
cards.why: The address bus (one-way, out of the CPU) says where: 100. The data bus (two-way) carries what: 42. The control bus carries signals such as 'write'.
cards.hook: Address = where, data = what, control = do it.
keys: The address bus (one-way, out of the CPU) says where

cards.q: Which memory is volatile: its contents are lost when the power is switched off?
cards.why: RAM is volatile, so it is wiped when the power goes. ROM, SSDs and hard drives are non-volatile: they keep their data with no power.
cards.hook: RAM forgets when the plug is pulled; ROM remembers.

cards.q: Which of these is normally stored in ROM?
wrong: Data moved out of a full RAM
cards.why: ROM is non-volatile and read-only, so it keeps the boot program that must survive with the power off. Open programs and documents are in RAM.
cards.hook: ROM: Read Only, and still there at switch-on.

cards.q: Which statement about registers and RAM is correct?
cards.right: Registers are inside the CPU and faster
wrong: Registers are slower, on the motherboard
Registers keep their data with no power
cards.why: Registers are built into the CPU, so they are the fastest memory, but a CPU has only a few of them, whereas RAM sits on the motherboard and holds gigabytes.
cards.hook: Registers: tiny, inside, instant.
keys: Registers are built into the CPU

cards.q: A laptop with 4 GB of RAM slows down when many programs are open. Why does adding more RAM help?
cards.right: Less swapping to slow virtual memory
wrong: It raises the CPU's clock speed
It gives more space to save files
Programs stay in RAM when it's off
cards.why: When RAM is full the OS moves data out to virtual memory on the much slower disk. More RAM means more fits at once, so there is less swapping.
cards.hook: RAM is the desk: a bigger desk, fewer trips to the filing cabinet.
keys: virtual memory on the much slower disk

cards.q: What is cache memory?
cards.right: Small, fast memory close to the CPU
wrong: Large, slow storage for saving files
Memory that keeps data with no power
The register holding the next address
cards.why: Cache is small, very fast memory in or next to the CPU. It holds instructions and data used often, so the CPU waits less for slower RAM.
cards.hook: Cache: keep what you use most within arm's reach.
keys: holds instructions and data used often

cards.q: Put these in order from fastest to slowest: RAM, registers, SSD, cache.
cards.why: The closer to the CPU, the faster (and smaller and dearer): registers are inside the CPU, then cache, then RAM on the motherboard, then the SSD.
cards.hook: Closest to the CPU is quickest: registers, cache, RAM, storage.
keys: registers are inside the CPU, then cache

cards.q: A CPU's clock runs at 2 GHz. How many clock cycles does it make in half a second?
cards.why: Giga means a billion (10⁹) and hertz means per second: 2 GHz is 2,000,000,000 cycles a second, so half a second is 1,000,000,000.
cards.hook: Clock speeds use 1000s: kilo, mega, giga, each × 1000.

cards.q: Two CPUs have the same clock speed. One has 4 cores and the other has 2. Why can the 4-core CPU get more done?
cards.right: It runs more instructions at once
wrong: Its clock ticks twice as fast
It has twice as much RAM
cards.why: Each core is a processor of its own, running its own fetch-decode-execute cycle, so 4 cores work on 4 instructions at the same time. The clock speed is the same.
cards.hook: Clock speed = how fast each worker is; cores = how many workers.
keys: 4 cores work on 4 instructions at the same time

cards.q: Why is a solid state drive (SSD) better than a hard disk drive (HDD) in a laptop that gets carried around?
cards.right: No moving parts, so it copes with knocks
wrong: It stores data on magnetic platters
It is volatile, so it uses less power
cards.why: An SSD stores data in flash memory chips with no moving parts, so a bump can't damage a spinning disk or a moving head. An HDD is cheaper per gigabyte.
cards.hook: Solid state: nothing spins, nothing breaks.

cards.q: Which of these is an embedded system?
cards.right: The microcontroller in a washing machine
wrong: A web server in a data centre
A desktop PC used for gaming
cards.why: An embedded system is a small computer built into a bigger device to do one dedicated job. Laptops, PCs and servers are general-purpose: they run any software.
cards.hook: Embedded = built in, one job.

cards.q: Which of these is true of an embedded system but not of a general-purpose computer?
cards.right: It does one job, often in real time
wrong: It can install and run any app
It needs a keyboard, mouse and screen
It uses lots of power and memory
cards.why: An embedded system is built for one dedicated job, so it can be small, cheap, low-power and react in real time. A PC must run anything, so it needs more.
cards.hook: One job, done fast and cheaply: that's embedded.

cards.q: Partway through a program the PC holds 7 and the accumulator holds 7. What does each 7 mean?
cards.right: PC: address 7 is next; ACC: the value 7
cards.why: The PC holds an address: the next instruction is at location 7. The accumulator holds data: 7 is the value the ALU has just worked out.
cards.hook: PC points somewhere; ACC holds something.

cards.q: Which logic gate outputs 1 only when both of its inputs are 1?
cards.why: AND gives 1 only for inputs 1 and 1; any 0 makes the output 0. OR gives 1 if at least one input is 1, and NAND is the opposite of AND.
cards.hook: AND is fussy: it needs this AND that.
keys: AND gives 1 only for inputs 1 and 1

cards.q: Inputs (A, B) go 00, 01, 10, 11. What is the output column of an OR gate, in that order?
cards.why: OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1, so only 00 gives 0: 0, 1, 1, 1. (0, 0, 0, 1 is AND and 0, 1, 1, 0 is XOR.)
cards.hook: OR is easy-going: either one will do.

cards.q: Which gate outputs 1 when exactly one of its two inputs is 1, but 0 when both are 1?
cards.why: XOR (exclusive OR) is 1 when the inputs are different. OR also gives 1 for 01 and 10, but it gives 1 for 11 too.
cards.hook: XOR: one or the other, but not both.
keys: XOR (exclusive OR) is 1 when the inputs are different

cards.q: What does a NAND gate output for inputs 1, 1 and for inputs 0, 1?
cards.why: NAND is AND then NOT. 1 AND 1 = 1, flipped to 0; 0 AND 1 = 0, flipped to 1. The small circle on its output is the NOT.
cards.hook: NAND = Not AND: do the AND, then flip it.

cards.q: Inputs (A, B) go 00, 01, 10, 11. What is the output column of a NOR gate, in that order?
cards.why: NOR is OR then NOT. OR gives 0, 1, 1, 1; flipping each gives 1, 0, 0, 0: the output is 1 only when both inputs are 0.
cards.hook: NOR = Not OR: work out OR, then flip every row.

cards.q: A logic gate is drawn with a flat back and a round, D-shaped front. Which gate is it?
cards.why: AND is D-shaped: flat back, round front. OR has a curved back and a pointed front, XOR adds an extra curved line, and NOT is a triangle.
cards.hook: D-shape = anD.

cards.q: How many rows does a truth table need for a circuit with 3 inputs?
cards.why: Each input can be 0 or 1, and each extra input doubles the rows: 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8 rows, from 000 to 111.
cards.hook: Rows = 2 to the power of the number of inputs.

cards.q: A half adder adds two bits, A and B. Which gate gives its carry bit C?
cards.why: A carry happens only for 1 + 1 = 10, when both bits are 1: that is A AND B. The sum bit S is A XOR B.
cards.hook: Carry only when both are 1: AND. Sum when they differ: XOR.

cards.q: A half adder has S = A XOR B and C = A AND B. What are S and C when A = 1 and B = 1?
cards.why: In binary 1 + 1 = 10. 1 XOR 1 = 0, so the sum digit S is 0, and 1 AND 1 = 1, so the carry C is 1.
cards.hook: 1 + 1 = 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1.

cards.q: What is a transistor?
cards.right: A tiny electronic switch: on 1, off 0
wrong: A chip with millions of components on it
A cell that keeps data with no power
A wire carrying data between CPU parts
cards.why: A transistor is a switch made from a semiconductor such as silicon: on lets current through (1), off doesn't (0). Logic gates are built from transistors.
cards.hook: Transistor = switch; billions of switches = a CPU.

cards.q: What is an integrated circuit?
cards.right: Many transistors on one silicon chip
wrong: A board that joins separate chips
The bus joining the CPU and RAM
cards.why: An integrated circuit puts many components, mostly transistors, together on one small chip of silicon. A CPU is an integrated circuit with billions of them.
cards.hook: Integrated = all built into one chip.
keys: on one small chip of silicon

cards.q: Why do computers store data in binary?
cards.right: Transistors have two states: on and off
wrong: Binary uses less memory than denary
Each transistor holds ten voltage levels
cards.why: A computer is built from transistors, switches that are either on (1) or off (0). Two states are easy to tell apart even if the voltage wobbles a little.
cards.hook: Two states, two digits: on = 1, off = 0.

cards.q: A chip has 2 billion transistors. Moore's Law says the number doubles about every 2 years. About how many will there be after 6 years?
cards.why: 6 years is 3 doublings of 2 years each: 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 billion. Doubling every single year would be wrong: the law says about every 2 years.
cards.hook: Count the doublings first: years ÷ 2.

cards.q: A push button and a temperature sensor are inputs to an embedded system. Which kind of signal does each give?
cards.why: A button is only ever pressed or not, two values (1 or 0): digital. Temperature varies smoothly across a range: analogue.
cards.hook: Digital = steps (on/off); analogue = a smooth dial.

cards.q: Which input row makes A AND (B OR C) equal 1?
cards.why: Work out the bracket first: B OR C must be 1, and then A must be 1 too. Only A = 1, B = 0, C = 1 gives 1 AND 1 = 1.
cards.hook: Brackets first, then the gate outside.

cards.q: In the 8-row truth table of A AND (B OR C), how many rows have output 1?
cards.why: A must be 1 (rows 100, 101, 110, 111) and B OR C must be 1, which rules out 100. That leaves 101, 110 and 111: 3 rows.
cards.hook: AND with A: cross out every row where A = 0 first.

cards.q: Which expression always has the same value as not (P and Q)?
cards.why: not (P and Q) is False only when P and Q are both True. not P or not Q is also False only then, so the two truth tables match.
cards.hook: Break the bracket: flip each letter and swap and ↔ or.
keys: False only when P and Q are both True

cards.q: (P, Q) go (F, F), (F, T), (T, F), (T, T). What is the column for not P or not Q, in that order?
cards.why: not P is T, T, F, F and not Q is T, F, T, F. OR is False only when both are False, which is the last row: T, T, T, F.
cards.hook: Flip first, then OR: only the all-False row gives False.
keys: OR is False only when both are False

cards.q: A and B each go through a NOT gate, and the two results go into an OR gate. Which single gate does this behave like?
cards.why: (NOT A) OR (NOT B) is 0 only when A and B are both 1, exactly like NAND: AND then NOT. The truth tables match row for row.
cards.hook: Flipped inputs into OR = NAND; flipped inputs into AND = NOR.

cards.q: Which Python condition is True only for points inside the square that runs from x = 0 to 5 and from y = 0 to 5?
cards.why: A point is inside only if it passes all four limits (left, right, bottom, top), so join them with and. With or, a point passing just the x test would count.
cards.hook: Inside a box: every limit must hold, so use and.

cards.q: What is an operating system?
wrong: An application, like a word processor
The CPU that runs the programs
The start-up program kept in ROM
cards.why: The OS (Windows, Linux, Android) is system software: it manages the CPU, memory, storage and devices, and is the interface between users, apps and hardware.
cards.hook: OS = the manager between you, your apps and the hardware.
keys: it manages the CPU, memory, storage and devices

cards.q: Which job of the operating system decides which program runs on the CPU next, and for how long?
cards.why: A core runs one process at a time, so the scheduler shares out CPU time (e.g. round robin), switching so fast that programs seem to run together.
cards.hook: Scheduling shares out the CPU's time; memory management shares out RAM.
keys: the scheduler shares out CPU time

cards.q: You save an essay as Hamlet.docx in a folder called English, then later rename it. Which job of the operating system looks after this?
cards.why: Saving puts the essay on storage. File management organises files on storage: their names, folders and where each is kept, and lets you create, rename and delete them.
cards.hook: Saved = on storage = file management.
keys: File management organises files on storage

cards.q: Round robin scheduling: programs A, B and C take turns on the CPU, 10 ms each, starting with A at 0 ms. Which runs from 30 ms to 40 ms?
wrong: None: each has had its turn
cards.why: Turns go A 0–10, B 10–20, C 20–30 ms, then back to A for 30–40 ms. Round robin keeps cycling until each program has finished.
cards.hook: Round robin: everyone gets a slice, then back to the front of the queue.

cards.q: A graphical user interface (GUI) is often called WIMP. What does WIMP stand for?
cards.why: A GUI shows windows, icons, menus and a pointer: you click or tap on pictures instead of typing commands as in a command line interface.
cards.hook: W-I-M-P: everything you see and point at on a desktop.
keys: windows, icons, menus and a pointer

cards.q: What is a protocol in networking?
wrong: The address of a device on a network
cards.why: A protocol is a set of agreed rules for formatting, addressing, sending and checking data, so devices from different makers understand each other.
cards.hook: Protocol = the shared language and manners of a network.

cards.q: What does HTTP do?
cards.right: Lets a browser request web pages
wrong: Turns a web address into an IP address
cards.why: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) lets a browser request a web page from a web server and the server send it back. DNS finds addresses; TCP makes the packets.
cards.hook: HTTP: hypertext = web pages, transfer = fetch them.
keys: lets a browser request a web page from a web server

cards.q: What does HTTPS add to HTTP?
wrong: A check that no packets are lost
cards.why: HTTPS is HTTP Secure: it sends the data through an encrypted SSL/TLS connection, so anyone who intercepts it sees only scrambled bytes.
cards.hook: S for Secure: scrambled on the way.

cards.q: You type your card number into a page whose address begins http:// rather than https://. What is the risk?
cards.right: It is sent unencrypted and can be read
wrong: The packets may arrive out of order
The site's IP address can't be found
The number is lost if a packet drops
cards.why: HTTP sends everything as plain, unencrypted text, so anyone who intercepts the packets can read the card number. HTTPS would encrypt it.
cards.hook: No S, no secret.

cards.q: A message is sent by TCP as packets 1 to 5. They arrive in the order 3, 1, 5, 2, 4. What happens?
cards.right: TCP reorders them by sequence number
wrong: It is shown in the order 3, 1, 5, 2, 4
The whole message is sent again
The router sorts them before delivery
cards.why: Packets can take different routes, so they arrive in any order. TCP numbers each one, and the receiver reassembles them in order using those sequence numbers.
cards.hook: Number the packets, and the order can't get lost.

cards.q: A TCP sender sends packets 1 to 6 but gets no acknowledgement for packet 4 before the timeout. What does it do?
cards.why: The receiver acknowledges each packet it gets. No acknowledgement before the timeout means packet 4 was lost, so the sender resends just that packet.
cards.hook: No 'got it' back? Send that one again.
keys: the sender resends just that packet

cards.q: Which protocol suits a live video call, where speed matters more than every packet arriving?
cards.why: UDP sends packets with no acknowledgements or resending, so it is fast and a lost packet is just a small glitch. TCP would pause to resend, causing lag.
cards.hook: UDP: fire and forget. TCP: check and resend.

cards.q: Which of these is a valid IPv4 address?
cards.why: An IPv4 address is four numbers 0 to 255 (8 bits each) with dots. 256 doesn't fit in 8 bits; 00:1A:… is a MAC address and www.example.ie is a domain name.
cards.hook: IPv4: four numbers, each from 0 to 255.

cards.q: Which address is fixed into a device's network card when it is made, and stays the same on any network?
cards.why: A MAC address is burned into the network card at the factory. An IP address is given by the network the device joins, so it can change.
cards.hook: MAC is made in the factory; IP is issued by the network.
keys: burned into the network card at the factory

cards.q: What does a DNS server do?
cards.right: Turns a domain name into an IP address
wrong: Encrypts data between browser and server
Gives each device its MAC address
cards.why: DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phone book: it looks up a name like rte.ie and returns its IP address. Routers, not DNS, forward the packets.
cards.hook: DNS: names in, numbers out.

cards.q: What does a router do?
wrong: Turns domain names into IP addresses
Stores the web pages of a site
Encrypts the data in each packet
cards.why: A router reads each packet's destination IP address and sends it on along the best route to the next network. DNS, not the router, finds IP addresses.
cards.hook: Router: it picks the route.
keys: reads each packet's destination IP address

cards.q: You type a web address. Put in order: (1) the server sends the page back, (2) DNS finds the server's IP address, (3) the browser sends an HTTP request.
cards.why: The browser needs the server's IP address before it can send anything, so DNS comes first (2). Then the HTTP request goes out (3) and the server replies (1).
cards.hook: Look up the number before you can call.

cards.q: In the client-server model, what does the client do?
cards.right: Sends requests and shows the replies
wrong: Stores the site and answers requests
cards.why: The client (e.g. your browser) sends a request; the server, a powerful computer waiting for requests, processes it and sends back a response.
cards.hook: Client asks, server serves.
keys: The client (e.g. your browser) sends a request

cards.q: In the TCP/IP model, which layer splits a message into numbered packets?
cards.why: The transport layer (TCP) splits the message into packets, numbers them and checks they all arrive. The network layer adds the IP addresses.
cards.hook: Application formats, transport packs, network addresses, link sends.
keys: The transport layer (TCP) splits the message into packets

cards.q: A class keeps all its project files in the cloud. Which of these is a real disadvantage?
wrong: Only one person can open each file
Files are wiped when a laptop is off
Files can only be opened on one device
cards.why: Cloud files sit on a provider's servers and are reached over the internet: everyone can open them from anywhere, but without a connection no one can reach the work.
cards.hook: The cloud is only as close as your internet connection.
keys: without a connection no one can reach the work

cards.q: How are the protocols IP and VoIP related?
cards.right: VoIP sends voice calls as IP packets
wrong: IP is one type of VoIP
VoIP uses phone lines, not the internet
They are two names for one protocol
cards.why: IP addresses and routes packets of any data. VoIP (Voice over IP) is one use of it: speech is digitised and sent as IP packets, as on WhatsApp calls.
cards.hook: VoIP = Voice over IP: IP is the road, voice is one kind of traffic.
